0.label: studded_grid_panel
0.description: A tall rectangle filled with even rows of raised studs (about 7 across, 17-18 down) under a small crossed top, at the far left of the door's top register. It mirrors the studded conical form (#29) at the far right of the same register.
0.iconography: Most likely beaded regalia — a beaded panel or bag of the kind reserved for kings and chiefs. Because it is a regular grid, it is also the door's best candidate for a count (to test by counting studs), but nothing yet ties the number to reigns or years.

1.label: archer_drawing_bow
1.description: A man in a tall conical cap drawing a bow, the bow's hatched limb and straight string shown as a large 'D', in the top register of the left leaf.
1.iconography: An archer: hunter or bowman. In the top, royal register he may stand for the king's hunters or the town's founding hunter — a common figure in Yoruba town histories.

2.label: kneeling_courtier
2.description: A kneeling man in a conical cap with his hands joined at the chest and a long whisk or blade over his shoulder, in the top register of the left leaf.
2.iconography: Kneeling with joined hands is the Yoruba posture of greeting and submission before a king; the object over the shoulder marks an official or messenger of the palace.

3.label: file_of_five_animals
3.description: Five small four-legged animals stacked one above another in a narrow strip at the right end of the left leaf's top register.
3.iconography: Livestock — horses, cattle or goats — counted out in a column: wealth, tribute or spoils. The stacking reads like a tally, which makes it a small test case for 'pattern as number'.

4.label: spearman
4.description: A standing man in a conical helmet holding an upright spear, first in the second register of the left leaf.
4.iconography: A warrior of the town's army; the conical cap is the door's constant mark for fighting men.

5.label: archer_with_quiver
5.description: A standing man in a conical helmet with a bow over his shoulder and a quiver of arrows at his waist, in the left leaf's second register.
5.iconography: A bowman: part of a file of archers (#5-#8) marching to the right, the older arm of Yoruba warfare alongside the new rifles lower down the door.

6.label: archer_with_quiver
6.description: Second archer of the file in the left leaf's second register: conical helmet, bow over the shoulder, quiver at the waist.
6.iconography: One of a counted file of archers; see #5.

7.label: archer_with_quiver
7.description: Third archer of the file in the left leaf's second register, carrying bow and quiver.
7.iconography: One of a counted file of archers; see #5.

8.label: archer_with_quiver
8.description: Last archer of the file at the right end of the left leaf's second register, bow and quiver like the others.
8.iconography: One of a counted file of archers; see #5.

9.label: column_of_small_scenes
9.description: A narrow strip at the left of the central register: a small capped figure holding up square plaques, a quadruped below it and a lozenge, stacked one above another.
9.iconography: Small tokens set beside the leader figure (#23): goods or tribute carried in (the plaques) and animals. Too small to read securely.

10.label: two_horses
10.description: Two horses stacked one above the other, filling the left end of the right leaf's second register, a small figure at their feet.
10.iconography: Horses were costly imports and the sign of cavalry and rank in Yorubaland (the power of old Ọ̀yọ́). Here they march with the warriors: the town's mounted strength.

11.label: roped_captives_with_headloads
11.description: Three men in conical caps walking in file, each with a box-like load on his head, a rope running from neck to neck, in the fifth register of the right leaf.
11.iconography: A coffle: captives tied at the neck carrying goods — the booty and the enslaved people taken in war. It is one of the clearest records of 19th-century Yoruba warfare in the collection.

12.label: file_of_warriors_under_fish_frieze
12.description: Four standing figures in pointed caps, one with long streaming hair or plume, holding staffs or guns, beneath a frieze of fish and lozenges, in the bottom register of the right leaf.
12.iconography: Warriors on the march, possibly with a captive or a priest (the long-haired figure). The fish frieze above may mark a river crossing or simply divide registers.

13.label: roped_captives_with_headloads
13.description: Four men walking in file with boxes on their heads and a rope held or tied at neck level, in the fifth register of the left leaf.
13.iconography: The left leaf's coffle of captives, answering #11 on the right leaf: people and goods taken in war, led home.

14.label: stacked_lozenge_emblem
14.description: A vertical column of lozenges and comb-like crossbars, upper half, beside the left leader figure (#23) in the central register.
14.iconography: An emblem or staff of office rendered in abstract form (compare beaded staffs and Ogboni emblems). Its partner below is #24.

15.label: warriors_over_small_animal
15.description: Two warriors in conical caps, one with a spear and one with a leaf-bladed sword, walking over a small animal at the bottom right corner of the right leaf.
15.iconography: Armed men on the march; the animal under their feet (dog, lizard or crocodile) may be a hunting dog or a register-filler.

16.label: rifleman
16.description: A standing man in a conical cap holding a long gun upright, its stock at his feet, at the left end of the fourth register of the left leaf, beside a zigzag band.
16.iconography: A rifleman — the first of a file (#30). Rifles date the carving to the later 19th century, the era of the Kiriji / Ekitiparapọ war in which Ado-Ekiti fought.

17.label: large_archer_with_crest
17.description: A larger standing figure with a tall crested cap, holding a bow, at the right of the right leaf's central register, beside a vertical zigzag band.
17.iconography: Bigger than the rank-and-file: a war leader or chief hunter. The zigzag beside him can be read as a serpent or as Ṣàngó's lightning.

18.label: ring_pierced_by_rod
18.description: A large oval ring crossed diagonally by a straight rod, in the top register of the right leaf beside the crowned figure (#28).
18.iconography: An emblem set among the regalia: possibly a snare or trap, a fan, or a ring-and-staff of office. Unclear.

19.label: spearmen_with_small_figure
19.description: Two warriors with spears walking, a small figure or club between them, in the bottom register of the right leaf.
19.iconography: Part of the returning or marching army; the small figure may be a child or captive.

20.label: rifleman_guard
20.description: A standing man in a conical cap holding a long gun, at the right end of the left leaf's fifth register, behind the captives (#13).
20.iconography: The guard who drives the captives: the rifle makes the scene one of capture, not procession.

21.label: captives_led_by_rifleman
21.description: Two roped men with headloads followed by a taller man holding an upright rifle, at the right of the right leaf's fifth register.
21.iconography: Captor and captives in one frame — the clearest statement on the door that these files are prisoners of war.

22.label: rifleman
22.description: A man in a tall cap holding a gun, at the far left of the left leaf's bottom register, beside a zigzag band.
22.iconography: The first of the bottom register's armed file (#35).

23.label: leader_with_crossed_bands
23.description: The largest figure on the left leaf: frontal, head framed in a triangle, arms raised to two broad bands that cross behind the body to the corners, flared triangular skirt, set in the centre of the door.
23.iconography: Scale and centrality mark a ruler or war chief. The crossed bands read as charm-laden bandoliers or a baldric worn by war leaders; the same figure on the right leaf (#34) makes a pair — perhaps the king and his war general, or two allied leaders.

24.label: stacked_lozenge_emblem
24.description: Lower half of the lozenge-and-crossbar column beside the left leader (#23), continuing #14.
24.iconography: Continuation of the emblem or staff at #14.

25.label: tortoise
25.description: A tortoise seen from above, its shell marked in a grid, in the top register of the right leaf; a second tortoise (#26) sits below it.
25.iconography: Ìjàpá the tortoise, the cunning trickster of Yoruba tales and a common offering; near the king it can signal wisdom and long life. A pair of tortoises may also be counted offerings.

26.label: tortoise
26.description: The second tortoise, below #25, same gridded shell, in the top register of the right leaf.

27.label: line_of_kneeling_figures
27.description: Seven kneeling figures with crested hair in one row, each reaching to the back of the figure in front, filling the third register of the right leaf.
27.iconography: Kneeling is greeting and submission. The linked hands and crested hair suggest either palace wives kneeling to the king or captives tied in a line; in a door so full of war, captives are likely.

28.label: crowned_king_with_attendants
28.description: A frontal figure wearing a crown with upright points, arms resting on two small attendants at his sides, in the top register of the right leaf.
28.iconography: A king supported by attendants is a classic royal image across Yoruba and Benin art. On a door captioned as the palace door of the ruler of Ado, this is most likely the Ewì himself at the head of the chronicle.

29.label: beaded_conical_crown
29.description: A tall conical form covered in rows of raised beads, closing at a pointed top, at the far right of the right leaf's top register; it mirrors the studded grid (#0) at the far left.
29.iconography: Most likely a beaded crown (adé) — the supreme emblem of a Yoruba king — placed beside the crowned figure. A maize cob (abundance) is the alternative reading.

30.label: file_of_six_riflemen
30.description: Six men in conical caps standing in file, each holding a long gun upright, in the fourth register of the left leaf.
30.iconography: A rifle company. Repeated identical figures read as a count of men — the army's strength — as much as a picture.

31.label: line_of_kneeling_figures
31.description: Six kneeling figures with crested hair, hands joined to the figure in front, filling the third register of the left leaf.
31.iconography: Mirror of #27 on the other leaf: submitting people — wives greeting the king or captives in a line.

32.label: crouching_monkey
32.description: A squatting animal with long limbs and a hand raised to its mouth, at the left of the right leaf's central register.
32.iconography: A monkey — in Yoruba lore a mimic and trickster, and in masquerade a figure of mockery. Beside the leader it may be a comic or cautionary aside.

33.label: swordsman
33.description: A man in a conical helmet holding a long straight sword upright, below the monkey on the right leaf's central register.
33.iconography: A sword-bearer or executioner in the leader's retinue.

34.label: leader_with_crossed_bands
34.description: The large frontal figure on the right leaf, triangle-framed head, raised arms and crossed bands — the mirror of #23.
34.iconography: The second leader. A pair of equal leaders at the centre of both leaves may record an alliance — for Ado-Ekiti, the Ekitiparapọ confederacy — or king and war chief.

35.label: file_with_tall_headgear
35.description: Six figures with tall cylindrical hats, holding guns or staffs, in the bottom register of the left leaf.
35.iconography: Men of rank or a different company: the tall hats set them apart from the conical-capped soldiers. Could also be carriers with loads.

36.label: file_of_armed_guards
36.description: Four men in conical caps holding guns and spears, at the right of the right leaf's second register, beside the horses (#10).
36.iconography: Armed escort of the mounted men; guns and spears together show the mixed weapons of the late-19th-century wars.

37.label: file_of_seven_riflemen
37.description: Seven men in conical caps with upright guns, the last one crouching, filling the fourth register of the right leaf.
37.iconography: The right leaf's rifle company, answering #30 (six men) on the left.

panel.title: Palace door of the Ewì of Ado-Ekiti: king, army and captives
panel.summary: A two-leaf door photographed by Frobenius and captioned as the palace door of the ruler of Ado. Seven registers per leaf run from a crowned king and regalia at the top, through archers, horsemen and riflemen, to captives roped at the neck carrying loads under armed guard.

register_readings.reading: The royal register: the crowned king supported by attendants (#28), beaded regalia at both ends (#0, #29), an archer, a kneeling courtier, a column of animals and two tortoises.
The army assembles: a spearman and four archers with quivers on the left; two horses and armed guards on the right.
Six and seven kneeling figures in linked lines — people submitting, likely captives or wives.
The centre: two large leaders with crossed bands, one per leaf, flanked by emblems, a monkey, a swordsman and a large crested archer.
Rifle companies: six men on the left, seven on the right, guns upright.
Captives with headloads tied neck to neck, driven by riflemen — the spoils of war.
The army on the march: men in tall hats, spearmen and swordsmen, a fish frieze above and a small animal below.

panel.composition: Two leaves read top to bottom in matching registers, with the king at the head and the two largest figures at the centre. Rank is shown by scale and headgear; each register repeats one type of person, so the door reads as counted groups.
panel.narrative: Read in order, the door tells the power of the Ado kingship through war: the crowned Ewì and his regalia; the army of archers, cavalry and riflemen; the two leaders; and the result — people kneeling in submission and captives led away with goods. Rifles and neck-roped coffles are period evidence of the 19th-century wars, when Ado-Ekiti fought in the Ekitiparapọ confederacy against Ibadan. The door is less a portrait of one battle than a record of the kingdom's strength and its captives.
panel.hypotheses: Strong support for 'chronicle' as a war record ordered from king to captives; a single king, not a king list. Moderate support for 'pattern as number': the counted files (4 archers, 6 and 7 kneeling, 6 and 7 riflemen, 5 animals, a studded grid) invite a tally reading that could be tested against oral accounts.
cross_panel_links: Riflemen and kneeling figures link it to the Ifá tray EBA-Div_00302, where armed men and couples share the rim.
Conical-capped standing figures in files recur on the Ife door leaves EBA-Div_00311 and EBA-Div_00312.
The crowned figure with attendants compares with the crowned mount-sheet figures KBA_19153-19157.
uncertainties: Several boxes cut groups arbitrarily (e.g. #16 inside #30, #19 and #15 overlapping #12), so some figures are counted twice.
The kneeling lines could be wives rather than captives; the crossed-band figures could be kings, war chiefs or masqueraders.
